Software that changes shifts at short notice is often presented as a scheduling tool. A manager enters demand, the system produces a roster, and workers receive an update (through an app, a text message, or an automated call). The claimed purpose is flexibility. The practical result can be a workplace in which the employer decides when work exists and the worker absorbs every consequence of that decision.

That distinction matters. An inconvenient schedule is a problem of timing. An unpredictable schedule is a problem of power. When a shift can move, disappear, or appear with little warning, the worker cannot reliably plan sleep, transportation, childcare, education, or a second job. The schedule becomes a moving boundary around ordinary life. It’s not merely information about work; it’s a demand that life remain permanently available to work.

The software does not need to issue an order in plain language. It can rank availability, flag refusals, record response times, or attach a reliability score to a person who cannot accept a last-minute change. Each feature may be described as neutral. Together, they create pressure. A worker who declines an unexpected shift may lose future hours. A worker who accepts may lose money arranging care or traveling twice in one day. The system turns uncertainty into a cost, then places that cost on the person with the least room to carry it.

This is why unpredictability is a form of control — it narrows the choices that remain usable. Formal freedom can survive on paper while practical freedom shrinks. A worker may technically refuse a shift, but refusal means risking income, a lower rating, or fewer invitations. The software does not have to say that the worker must comply. It can make every alternative expensive.

The ordinary situations expose the gap. What happens when a shift moves after a caregiver has arranged coverage? What happens when a worker is called in during a scheduled class (or while traveling to another job)? What happens when an algorithm treats a person’s inability to answer within minutes as a lack of commitment? These are not unusual edge cases. They are the conditions under which a schedule becomes a disciplinary instrument.

Employers may say that rapid changes help them respond to demand. That may be true in a narrow operational sense. A store, warehouse, hospital, or delivery service can face changing needs. But flexibility for an institution is not automatically flexibility for the people who perform the work. When the employer keeps the ability to revise the plan and the worker keeps the obligation to adapt, the arrangement is flexible on one side only.

The central question is who controls the risk. If software improves forecasting, its gains should support stable notice, predictable hours, and compensation for changes made after a schedule is posted. A system that can identify a staffing problem can also identify who created the disruption (including the time, the reason, and the resulting loss). It’s a choice whether that record becomes a tool for discipline or evidence for accountability.

Workers and labour organisers should demand rules that treat notice as a condition of employment, not a courtesy. A posted shift should carry weight. Changes should require a real threshold, clear communication, and pay when the employer changes the bargain. Workers should be able to decline last-minute assignments without retaliation, and they should be able to inspect the data used to evaluate availability (including the records behind a rating or penalty). A disclaimer cannot turn an unstable system into a fair one. It’s a smokescreen if the underlying incentives remain untouched.

We need collective standards because an individual refusal carries a different risk from an organised demand. We’re asking for control over time, and that means bargaining over the software that allocates it. You can bring the schedule to a union meeting, a workplace committee, or a public hearing and ask who benefits from each change, who pays for it, and what remedy follows. The governing principle is simple: technology may help coordinate work, but it should not make workers live on call. The next decision is whether the schedule serves the people who depend on it.
